chapter_theme: Sirupanatruppadai: a bard who has been enriched by Nalliyakkodan, chief of Oymanadu, directs a hungry fellow bard and his troupe to him, first measuring the patron against the three crowned cities and the seven famous givers, then promising the food of each land on the road to his town and the gifts he gives before he is asked.
structure_note: The poem moves from the road and the troupe (1-40) to the address to the suppliant, the three crowned cities set down as empty (41-83), the seven givers (84-113) and the patron who bore their yoke alone (114-129); then the speaker's own former poverty (130-145), three roads through neythal, mullai and marutham each ending in a meal (146-195), the patron's town (196-202), his virtues as four audiences praise them (203-220), the praise song (221-234), the gifts (235-260) and the patron's kurinji hill (261-269).

pattupattu:3:1-12.reading: The poem opens on the summer road the suppliants are walking: a forest river that once wound like the necklace swaying on the breast of the earth, a woman whose broad shoulders are gem-bearing hills, has left on its bank flowers the koels shook down and fine dark sand rippled like spread hair, and that sand has grown hot as heated iron, so that the travellers, stepping lightly over pebbles that tear their feet in the late days of summer under the driving morning sun, rest in the striped shade of a maraa tree on the long paalai road.
pattupattu:3:1-12.nuance: Line 11 says பாலை நின்ற பாலை: the paalai tree standing on the paalai road, or the paalai season standing over it; the pun is the poem's own. The bard will play the paalai mode on this same road at line 36, so land, season and music are tuned to one another. The river is dry here only by implication: its sand is described, not its water.
pattupattu:3:1-12.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 1-16, which ended inside the word சாஅய் (lines 16-17). Lines 1 to 12 are the road and the rest in the shade; line 12 ends with அசைஇ, and line 13 begins the description of the women who rest there.

thinai_evidence.note: the suppliants' journey on the road, the frame of the guide poem; no love situation

comparisons.tenor: the winding forest river across the land
the fine dark ripples of the river sand
the heat of the sun-baked sand

pattupattu:3:13-31.reading: The women dancers of the troupe are described feature by feature, each surpassing a thing of the land: their oiled dark hair outdoes the train that peacocks spread in the thin rain, so that the peacocks hide before their grace; their small feet are lovely as a tired dog's tongue; their thighs are closer and smoother than a she-elephant's trunk; the knot of their hair shines like the plantain's flower; bees drawn to the vengai's fresh blossom buzz at the spots on their skin; their breasts mock the kongu bud; their teeth drip sweetness like the palmyra's young fruit; and they are gentle, deer-eyed and bright-browed, with a chastity full as the mullai that opens in the kullai woodland.
pattupattu:3:13-31.nuance: The figure repeated through the passage (கதுப்பிற் கதுப்பு, குறங்கிற் குறங்கு, எயிற்றின் எயிறு, முலை முலை) sets each feature against a thing of the land that it surpasses, so the women are praised by making the forest yield to them; the frame returns at lines 263 and 264, where the peacocks of the patron's hill spread their trains like women's hair. The comparison of the feet to a tired dog's tongue is one of the poem's boldest: softness and redness, taken from the road's own weariness.
pattupattu:3:13-31.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16, 17-26 and 27-42, whose cuts at 16 and 26 fall inside the description (16 splits சாஅய், 26 ends one item of a list). Lines 13 to 31 are one catalogue of the women's beauty, closed by the noun விறலியர் in line 31.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the troupe's dancing women inside the praise poem; no love situation

comparisons.tenor: the knot of the women's hair (ஓதி)
the spots on the women's skin (சுணங்கு)

pattupattu:3:32-40.reading: While untaught young men gently stroke the small soft feet of the women, worn out by walking, the skilled bard holds on his left side the small sweet-voiced lute with strings tight-twisted like drawn gold and plays the paalai mode as its rule requires; and the guide turns to the addressee: old-mouthed suppliant, who has put weariness behind you though grief and longing for the generous in an unmoving world drive you along the road.
pattupattu:3:32-40.nuance: Line 38 இயங்கா வையத்து is hard: either a world that does not move to help, or a world in which the generous do not go about; both make the suppliant's search the cause of his grief. The address முதுவாய் இரவல, the suppliant of seasoned speech, is the same phrase the god's attendants use of the devotee in Thirumurugatruppadai line 284.
pattupattu:3:32-40.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 27-42: the vocative முதுவாய் இரவல in line 40 ends the opening frame, and line 41 begins the comparison of the three crowned cities.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide addresses a suppliant bard: the opening of the guide poem's speech

pattupattu:3:41-50.reading: In the western land, a wide-mouthed buffalo that has grazed the broad-petalled blue lilies, making the fat fish scatter, lies chewing on a bed of wild jasmine in the shade of jackfruit trees climbed by green pepper vines, with soft turmeric leaves stroking its hairy back and the scent of young toddy about it; yet even Vanji, with flood-water at its gate, the city of Kuttuvan of the well-made chariot, the descendant of the western guardians whose bar-like shoulders carved the curved bow on the northern Himalaya, is set down as empty.
pattupattu:3:41-50.nuance: வறிதே can mean that Vanji is small beside the patron the poem will name, or that it was barren for suppliants like these; the three cities are dismissed in the same words (lines 50, 67, 83) before the poem says what they are measured against, so the comparison is held back for more than seventy lines. The Chera's mark on the Himalaya is the boast that the Chera bow was carved there.
pattupattu:3:41-50.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 27-42 and 43-58: lines 41 to 50 are the Chera land and its city, closed by வஞ்சியும் வறிதே in line 50.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a crowned king's land used as a foil inside the guide poem

comparisons.tenor: the patron's giving, to which the poem builds

pattupattu:3:51-67.reading: Young female monkeys, decked like children with carved chest-pieces of old honey-dripping nunavu wood and made flower chaplets set at the ear, come with the strong-oxen carts of the salt merchants and play rattle, with pearls from the sea like teeth taken from the bellies of sharp-edged shells, together with the ornamented sons born to the salt women whose loose five-part hair hides their shoulders: such is the wave-bounded Korkai of the Pandya Seliyan, descendant of the southern guardians, of the swift chariot, eye-filling chaplet and garlanded white umbrella that took the enemies' land; yet even Madurai, of his unbearable lineage in which Tamil found its standing, its streets soaked in revelry, is set down as empty.
pattupattu:3:51-67.nuance: Monkeys playing with pearls beside the salt carts makes the pearl a toy: the wealth of Korkai is shown by how carelessly it is handled. தமிழ்நிலை பெற்ற in line 66 ties the standing of Tamil to the Pandya lineage and its city, though the poem says it only in passing, as an epithet.
pattupattu:3:51-67.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 43-58 and 59-79: lines 51 to 67 are the Pandya land and its city, closed by மதுரையும் வறிதே in line 67.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a crowned king's land used as a foil inside the guide poem

pattupattu:3:68-83.reading: On the bank of a fragrant pond beside a ford lovely as a painting, where kadamba garlands rise from the thick water, the divine lotus opens its face, its rich bud like a young breast, its pollen-covered outer petals red as the cochineal insect, and its golden seed-head wrapped in red petals like a flawless palm dipped in lac, while a bee, ruffling its wings and clasping its sweet mate, sings the kaamaram tune: such is the cool field country of the Chola Sembiyan, descendant of the eastern guardians, of the good chariot and fame that need not be sought, whose bangled hand destroyed the hanging fort whose high gates the thunder scrapes; yet even Uranthai, of his unretreating resolve, is set down as empty.
pattupattu:3:68-83.nuance: Each of the three cities is entered through one small scene of its land (the buffalo of the west, the monkeys of the south, the lotus and bee of the east) and each king through his ancestors and one deed; the pattern makes the three crowned dynasties a single formula that the patron, a minor chief, is then said to exceed.
pattupattu:3:68-83.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 59-79 and 80-98: lines 68 to 83 are the Chola land and its city, closed by உறந்தையும் வறிதே in line 83.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a crowned king's land used as a foil inside the guide poem

comparisons.tenor: the red petals round the seed-head

pattupattu:3:84-113.reading: The seven givers of old are named by their gifts: Pekan, chief of the Aviyar of the hill land guarded by a fearsome goddess, who gave a cloak to the forest peacock; Pari of Parambu, where white falls drop, who gave his great chariot to the small-flowered mullai on the long road; Kaari of the flashing spear, who gave suppliants horses with ringing bells and white manes and kind words that amazed the world; Aay, of loving speech and bow-bearing shoulders, who gave the god under the banyan the cloth the shining blue serpent had given him; Athikan of the roaring army, who gave Avvai the sweet nectar-yielding nelli fruit of the fragrant slope; Nalli of the dense hill, who gave his friends without stint the means to live; and Ori of the horse Ori, who fought Kaari of the horse Kaari and gave the performers a good land of hillocks: these seven together wore the red yoke of giving.
pattupattu:3:84-113.nuance: Several of the gifts are useless to the receiver (a cloak to a peacock, a chariot to a creeper, a god's cloth to a god): the list praises giving that does not weigh the receiver's need. Two of the seven, Kaari and Ori, are named as having fought each other (line 110), yet they share one yoke; the rivalry of chiefs is set aside in the canon of givers. The next unit says the patron bore alone the yoke the seven bore together.
pattupattu:3:84-113.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 80-98, 99-112 and 113-128: the list of the seven runs from line 84 to ஈகைச் செந்நுகம் in line 113, the noun that sums it up; the cuts at 98 and 112 fall inside it.

thinai_evidence.note: the catalogue of the seven famous givers, praise by precedent

comparisons.tenor: giving as a burden borne together

pattupattu:3:114-129.reading: He who alone, with strong legs and strength, bore that yoke so that the sea-fenced wide world shone is the great chief of the Oviyar, best among the kings of good Mavilangai (named after ancient Ilangai, where the dashing river brings fragrant naagam, agil and sandal that serve the bathing women as floats), with a true sword without blemish, the strength of a pouncing tiger, anklets on feet scarred by the elephant, and a hand that pours like rain and scatters herds of she-elephants as gifts: Nalliyakkodan, the famed patron of the many-instrumented performers; desiring him, we sang him, his father of unbearable lineage and the wealth of his sky-touching hill, and went to him the other day.
pattupattu:3:114-129.nuance: Here the comparison held back since line 50 is completed: the yoke seven wore together, this one bore alone (ஒருதான் தாங்கிய), and the three crowned cities were 'empty' beside it. The town is said to carry the name of ancient Ilangai, a claim about the name and not about the place.
pattupattu:3:114-129.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 113-128 and 129-148: line 113 ends the list of the seven, and the sentence about the patron runs to சென்றனமாக in line 129; the rest of line 129 (இந்நாள்) begins the next unit's scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron named and praised: his lineage, valour and giving

pattupattu:3:130-145.reading: In our dreary kitchen a new-whelped bitch, unable to bear her blind, droop-eared puppies tugging at her milkless teats, barked; under old walls with rotting rafters eaten by swarms of termites a hollow-stemmed mushroom grew in the dust; and the kinai-drummer's wife, her waist shrunk by settled hunger, nipped with her nails rubbish-heap velai greens, boiled them without salt and, ashamed before the gaze of the ignorant, shut the door to eat them with all her large family; so that this ruinous hunger might end, we got small-eyed elephants with streaming temples and bells at their sides and great chariots, and are coming from there; you too, with the large family that waits here in hope, if you go with a lifted heart . . .
pattupattu:3:130-145.nuance: The poverty is shown by what is missing in the kitchen (milk, salt, fire) and by the shame that makes the woman shut the door: hunger is also a public disgrace. The gift (elephants and chariots) is out of all proportion to the need for food, which is the point of the comparison with the seven givers.
pattupattu:3:130-145.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-148 and 149-164: the poverty scene and the gift run from line 130 to the conditional செல்குவிராயின் in line 145, which opens the road to the patron's country (lines 146 onward).

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's own former poverty and the patron's gift, offered to the hearer as proof

pattupattu:3:146-163.reading: On the long neythal road worthy of song, where the screwpine on the waves blooms white as swans, the first-day serunthi mimics gold, the full-swollen mundagam sheds bright gems, the tall punnai sets out pearls and the sea roams over the white sand of the shore grove, if you go to the port town of cool pools, named for its wall, the fishermen will light a red fire with black smoke from fragrant driftwood the waves brought in, lying like tall camels asleep, and pour you old clear toddy strained by a fisher-girl with a faultless face that makes the moon pine and spear-tip eyes; singing the noble lord of Kidangil with his bud-opened garland, and dancing to the beat with your women of sand-dark hair, you will get roast dried fish at every halt.
pattupattu:3:146-163.nuance: The town is named only by a riddle (named with the word for wall, மதிலொடு பெயரிய), which the reader is expected to solve as Eyil-pattinam. The camel, a beast of no Tamil landscape, is used as the image for logs on the beach. The patron is first named here as lord of Kidangil, the town the three roads lead to.
pattupattu:3:146-163.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-148 and 149-164: the neythal road and its welcome run from line 146 to பெறுகுவிர் in line 163, the first of the poem's three 'you will get' promises.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide promises the hospitality of the patron's coastal country

comparisons.tenor: the driftwood logs on the shore

pattupattu:3:164-177.reading: In the mullai woodland full of mullai, where the green-budded avarai strings corals, the dark-budded kaayaa opens like a flock of peacocks, the rich musundai creeper spreads, the clustered kaanthal blooms like fingers and cochineal insects crawl on the long field road, if, watching for the hour when the hill, bathed by falls from its clefts, has lost the sun's heat, you reach victorious Velur with its well that flowered at a spear's tip, you will get, in huts bright and shrivelled by the fierce sun, hot rice soured with sweet tamarind cooked by the hunter women, with roast wild cow, shared with your company of few bangles and mango-coloured skin.
pattupattu:3:164-177.nuance: Line 172, the well that 'flowered at the tip of a mighty spear', points to a story of a well opened with a spear, which the poem does not tell. The flowers listed (kaayaa, kaanthal, the cochineal after rain) are signs of the rains, so the road has passed from the summer of the opening to the wet season without saying so.
pattupattu:3:164-177.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 149-164 and 165-180: the mullai road and its welcome run from line 164 to பெறுகுவிர் in line 177.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide promises the hospitality of the patron's woodland country

pattupattu:3:178-195.reading: In the cool marutham fields full of marutham, where a blue kingfisher with a golden beak, having sat long on a bough of the short-stemmed kaanji whose fresh branch looks like a strung garland, watching the deep pool, snatches a stinking kayal fish, its sharp claws scarring the green lotus leaf, and a dark red-eyed male bee taking pollen on the opening lotus looks like the serpent seizing the moon, if you reach his Amur, the great guarded town of the brahmins with its lovely cool moat, the ploughmen's sister, her braid hanging on her small back like a she-elephant's trunk, will stop you as kin and give you heaps of white rice, well pounded by a black pestle with a worn iron mouth, with a mixture of forked-legged crab.
pattupattu:3:178-195.nuance: The three roads go through neythal, mullai and marutham in turn, each called 'full of' its own name (நெய்தல் 151, முல்லை சான்ற 169, மருதஞ் சான்ற 186), and each ends in a meal of its land; the patron's hill (kurinji) is reached last, at line 267, so his country holds all the lands. Which creature is the red-eyed male of line 184 is not certain; a bee fits the image of a dark thing on a bright flower.
pattupattu:3:178-195.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 165-180 and 181-202: the marutham road and its welcome run from line 178 to பெறுகுவிர் in line 195; line 196 begins a new sentence about the patron's own town.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide promises the hospitality of the patron's field country

comparisons.tenor: the dark bee on the bright lotus

pattupattu:3:196-202.reading: His festive old town, whose streets have their dust laid by the streams from his great war elephants, their broad feet with huge nails reddened by trampling corpses like the look of a ghoul-woman laughing after eating fat, with a tongue like overturned fire, gleaming teeth, ears like black kids' and forked feet, is not far: it is quite near.
pattupattu:3:196-202.nuance: The ghoul feeding on the battlefield, a figure of the war poems, is used here to measure the redness of an elephant's feet in a town at festival: the patron's violence abroad is the guarantee of the peace in which suppliants are fed. The streams that lay the dust (அருவி) may be the elephants' ichor or water they spray; the line does not decide.
pattupattu:3:196-202.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 181-202: lines 196 to 202 are one sentence, the patron's own town, which ends with நணியதுவே in line 202.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's war elephants and festive town

comparisons.tenor: the elephants' feet reddened by corpses

pattupattu:3:203-220.reading: Approaching the hard threshold of his gate, which is never shut to war-bards, poets or brahmins with the rare Veda on their tongues, open like the eye of a god's great hill, you will find him seated among his smiling company like the full moon among many stars: the wise praise him for knowing a favour done, keeping no low company, a glad face and a sweet manner; warriors of sword-sharp speech praise him for shielding those in fear, freedom from fierce anger, entering the enemy's array and holding a breaking army; women with lovely kohled eyes praise him for finishing what he purposes, being loved, not leaning to one side and understanding what has passed; and suppliants who live by gifts praise him for seeming simple in his knowledge while knowing well, knowing each one's due and giving without limit.
pattupattu:3:203-220.nuance: The virtues come in four sets of four, each set closed by the people who praise it (அறிந்தோர் ஏத்த, வயவர் ஏத்த, அரிவையர் ஏத்த, பரிசிலர் ஏத்த): the poem divides one man's character among the audiences who know it best. The suppliants praise last and praise two things about judgement (knowing each one's due) before the limitless giving that concerns them most. அறிவுமடம் படுதல் in line 216, knowledge that consents to seem simple, is a rare phrase.
pattupattu:3:203-220.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 203-217 and 218-233: the approach and the four praises run from line 203 to இருந்தோற் குறுகி in line 220, where the hearer reaches the patron; the cut at 217 falls in the middle of the fourth praise.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's virtues, praised by four kinds of people

comparisons.tenor: the gate that is never shut

pattupattu:3:221-234.reading: Holding your lute, whose stem with its bands is tight like a green-eyed langur gripping a snake, its mouth set with beauty like a row of gems, its bowl smoothly joined and covered with famed leather the colour of the forest kumizh fruit, its strings tight-twisted and oozing nectar, tune it by the rule of the treatise, voice answering voice, with the learning of one who has mastered the modes, and sing without tiring: 'you have a hand folded before elders, a chest open to the young, a sceptre that shades the ploughmen and a spear that burns the chariot warriors.'
pattupattu:3:221-234.nuance: The four praises are two pairs of opposites (folded and open; shade and fire), each pair setting a gentle gesture toward one's own people against a fierce one toward others; the poem gives the bard the words of his praise, so the guide also teaches what to say.
pattupattu:3:221-234.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 218-233 and 234-255: the lute and the praise song run from line 221 to வேலினை எனவும் in line 234; line 235 (நீ சில மொழியா அளவை) begins the sentence of the gifts.

thinai_evidence.note: the suppliant's praise song to the patron

comparisons.tenor: the lute's stem bound by its bands
the leather of the lute's bowl
the sweetness of the strings' sound

pattupattu:3:235-260.reading: Before you have said those few words, he will dress you in flawless cloth like the peeled skin of bamboo, give you toddy fierce as an angry snake, stand and feed you himself with endless care, from shining gold vessels set round like planets about the young sun and mocking it, the many foods of the subtle treatise written by the snow-hill-chested elder brother of the famed one with the flowered girdle whose forked arrows fed fire to the grove; and after ending the distress of connoisseurs and bards with the treasure his warriors brought from driving out enemies and razing kings' forts, he will give you a chariot whose wheel, its hub scarred by the sharp chisel and its spokes ringed by an iron rim, is like the full moon with its halo spreading milk-white rays in the seasonal sky, its covering of poured lac like the crowded buds of the tall murukku opening, finished by the iron-smiths' craft, with famed drivers of fine gait, draught beasts strong enough to outrun horses, and a charioteer.
pattupattu:3:235-260.nuance: The gift comes before the request (நீ சில மொழியா அளவை): the patron does not wait to be asked, which is the virtue the suppliants praised (வரையாது கொடுத்தல்). The cook-book author of lines 238 to 241 is described, not named, as the elder brother of a famed archer whose arrows fed fire to a grove; read as Bhima and Arjuna, it is a Mahabharata allusion inside a Tamil guide poem, and the food is said to follow that treatise to the letter.
pattupattu:3:235-260.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 234-255 and 256-269: the gifts run from நீ சில மொழியா அளவை in line 235 to தரீஇ in line 260, the verb of the chariot gift; line 261 begins the closing sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's gifts: cloth, drink, food and a chariot

comparisons.tenor: the chariot wheel with its rim
the lac-red covering of the chariot

pattupattu:3:261-269.reading: He sends you off that very day with his gift: go, if you desire Nalliyakkodan, lord of the kurinji with a chaplet of plucked shoots and a nature in which far-going fame has settled, whose peaks of swaying bamboo, where clear clouds creep and blue peacocks spread their trains in the mist like the soft lovely hair that women with swaying gait and fine-clothed hips spread to take agil smoke, rise to a summit hard to climb where the thunder strikes and passes.
pattupattu:3:261-269.nuance: The poem ends where it began: in lines 13 to 16 the women's hair outdid the peacock's train, and here the peacocks spread their trains like the women's hair, so the comparison is turned round at the patron's hill. The last line closes the conditional opened at line 145 (செல்குவிராயின் . . . செலினே): the whole road and every gift hang on the hearer's going.
pattupattu:3:261-269.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 256-269: the closing sentence begins with அன்றே விடுக்கும் in line 261 and ends the poem at line 269.

thinai_evidence.note: the close of the guide poem: the patron's hill and the final direction

links.note: The guide here calls the bard he directs முதுவாய் இரவல (line 40); in Thirumurugatruppadai line 284 the god's attendants announce the devotee to Murugan in the same words, முதுவாய் இரவலன்.
links.teaches: The same title for a seasoned suppliant names a bard seeking a chief in one guide poem and a devotee seeking the god in another, so the devotional guide poem approached Murugan through the bard's petition at a patron's gate and kept even its form of address.

links.note: Both describe Kuttuvan's western land by a buffalo that leaves the lotus pond to rest in jackfruit shade; Akananuru 91 says the hero will not stay for it even if he gains it, and the idyll calls even Kuttuvan's Vanji empty.
links.teaches: The buffalo resting in the jackfruit shade was a set emblem of the Chera land's ease, and both genres used it as the standard of plenty that is outweighed: by the heroine's beauty in the love poem and by a minor chief's giving in the guide poem.

links.note: Both name the seven givers (Pari, Ori, Kaari or Malaiyan, Athikan or Ezhini, Pekan, Aay, Nalli), with the shared formula for Pekan's hill guarded by a fearsome god (அருந்திறல் அணங்கின் / அருந்திறல் கடவுள்) and the same closing என ஆங்கு எழுவர.
links.teaches: The seven were a fixed list with stock epithets that a poet could set before a living patron, and the two poems use it differently: Perunchithiranar says the seven are dead so Kumanan must take their place, while the idyll says Nalliyakkodan already bears alone the yoke the seven bore together.

links.note: Avvai praises Athiyaman for giving her the nelli fruit without saying what it would do for him; the idyll lists Athikan as the giver of the nectar-yielding fruit to Avvai.
links.teaches: Avvai's poem makes the hiddenness of the fruit's virtue the point of the gift, whereas the idyll names that virtue openly (அமிழ்துவிளை), so by the time the story joined the list of seven the secret had become its public meaning.

links.note: Paranar cites Pekan's gift of a cloak to a peacock as proof that his giving looks to others' need and not to merit in the next world; the idyll lists the same gift as Pekan's emblem among the seven.
links.teaches: In Purananuru 141 the peacock's cloak is evidence in an argument about why a chief gives, while in the idyll it is only the sign by which Pekan is recognised, so a deed that once carried a claim about motive could circulate as a bare token of liberality.

links.note: Both show a bard's hunger by a mushroom growing in a cold kitchen (ஆம்பி) and a starving woman and her children; Perunthalai Saathanar shows it to Kumanan as his present state, the idyll's guide as a past state the patron ended.
links.teaches: The same kitchen of poverty serves as a petition in the Purananuru poem and as testimony in the guide poem, which shows how the guide form works: the bard's own former misery, once relieved, becomes the credential that sends another bard to the same patron.

links.note: The Kural says a ruler easy to see and not harsh of speech has his land praised above others; the idyll praises a gate never shut to bards, poets and brahmins, a glad face and freedom from fierce anger, each praised by a named class of people.
links.teaches: The Kural's abstract reward of praise has a concrete source in the idyll, where the people at the open gate (wise men, warriors, women and suppliants) are the ones who do the praising, so accessibility is rewarded by the very classes it admits.

links.note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbending sceptre; the bard's song praises both, the sceptre that shades the ploughmen and the spear that burns the chariot warriors.
links.teaches: The bard gives sceptre and spear equal places by assigning them to different people, subjects and enemies, while the Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear even in war, so the ethical book turns the praise poem's balanced pair into a hierarchy.

source_issues: Line 49 prints குட்டுவண் for the king's name, elsewhere குட்டுவன் (a ண/ன confusion); the entity copies the printed form.
Line 116 prints நாககு, which reads as a misprint for நாகமும் (the list நாகமும் அகிலும் ஆரமும்); the karu form copies the printed text.
Line 52 prints தறைவாய்த் குறுந்துணி: a த் before கு is irregular; expected அறைவாய்க் (or the like).
Lines 50 and 83 print யதாஅன்று but line 67 prints யுதாஅன்று for the same connective (அதாஅன்று).
Line 131 prints கறவாக் பால்முலை, where sandhi expects கறவாப் பால்முலை.
Line 139 prints இருக்பே ரொக்கலொ, which reads as a misprint for இரும்பேர் ஒக்கலொடு (as at line 144, இரும்பே ரொக்கற்).
Line 145 prints செம்ம லூள்ளமொடு with ஊ, where உள்ளம் expects லுள்ளமொடு.
Line 152 prints மணிநீர்ப் வைப்பு: a ப் before வ is irregular.
Line 245 prints றனின் றூட்டி; தான் நின்று ஊட்டி expects றானின் றூட்டி.
Line 242 சூழ்த்த may be a misprint for சூழ்ந்த.
